opus-5.5.text:
I'd push back a little on "general-purpose." I see the hash-based eval as a clean stress test of one specific thing that most long-context benchmarks fail to isolate, not as a complete measure of long-context ability.

The problem with a lot of earlier evals, like needle-in-a-haystack, is that the needle is semantically odd. You drop a sentence about pizza into a pile of essays, and the model can find it because it sticks out. So you end up measuring whether the model can spot an anomaly, not whether it's actually using the whole context.

Hashes avoid that. They're random, so there's no semantic signal and nothing to compress. Every pair looks the same as every other pair, so the model can't shortcut its way to the answer with priors or salience. If it gets it right, it genuinely stored and retrieved that information from context.

The multi-hop part matters even more. If you ask the model to follow a chain, hash one points to hash two, which points to hash three, and you shuffle the pairs so they're scattered across the context, it can't solve the task by attending to one location. It has to compose several lookups across the full window. That's much closer to what we care about for something like code, where understanding one function means jumping to a definition somewhere else, then to a type defined elsewhere, and so on. You can also make it harder by asking the model to skip straight to the end of the chain without writing out the intermediate steps, which tests whether it can do that composition internally.

What it doesn't tell you is whether the model does anything useful with real, messy data: whether it reasons well, writes good code, or knows what's relevant. So I think of it as a necessary condition. If a model can't do multi-hop retrieval over random hashes at a hundred million tokens, I don't believe its long-context claims. If it can, that's a strong signal the architecture works, and then you still need real-world tasks to see if it's actually smart with that context.

r001.rationale: The response says hashes are random, have no semantic signal, and cannot be answered using semantic priors or salience.

r002.rationale: It discusses retrieval hops and scattered context, but does not identify context coverage and hop count as the central quantitative dimensions of general-purpose long-context ability; it instead calls the hash eval a test of one specific capability.

r003.rationale: It separates hash-based retrieval and composition from abilities such as reasoning, coding, and relevance judgments, which it says require real-world tasks to evaluate.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'd push back a little on the framing, because I don't think it's a good general-purpose measure of long-context ability, and that's kind of the point of it. We built the hash-based eval because the existing benchmarks were measuring the wrong thing. Needle-in-a-haystack tells you whether a model can find one salient fact in a sea of irrelevant text. That's a retrieval problem, and attention is basically built to solve it. Models saturate it and people walk away thinking they have a million tokens of usable context, when in practice the model falls apart at thirty or forty thousand on anything that requires real reasoning.

So what the hash eval does is strip out everything that lets a model cheat. You take random hashes, so there's no semantic prior, no way to guess from world knowledge what the answer should be. And then you chain them. Hash one points to hash two, hash two points to hash three, and you ask the model to follow that chain across the full context. Now it's not enough to attend to one location. The model has to find something, hold it, use it to find the next thing, and keep that going. Every step is a place where it can lose the thread.

What I like about it is that it's a lower bound. It's deliberately adversarial. If a model can do multi-hop reasoning over random content it has no reason to have memorized, you can be fairly confident that the easier, more natural cases will work too. The reverse isn't true. Passing a benchmark with semantically meaningful text tells you very little, because you can't separate what the model retrieved from what it just knew. So I'd call it a good measure of whether the context window is actually usable, rather than nominally there. For a lot of what we care about at Magic, code understanding across a repository, that's the question that matters, and it's the one most benchmarks were quietly skipping.

r001.rationale: It says random hashes provide “no semantic prior” and prevent guessing from world knowledge, explaining that semantic information is removed.

r002.rationale: It describes following a chain across the full context, but does not identify context coverage and the number of sequential retrieval hops as the central quantitative dimensions.

r003.rationale: It mentions repository code understanding as a use case, but does not distinguish abilities measured by general-purpose context evaluation from those better measured by domain-specific evaluations.

astra-6.text:
The intuition is that it tests whether the model can actually access information throughout its context, without being able to guess the answer from prior knowledge. You give it a large number of random hash pairs, and then ask for the value associated with a particular key. Because those associations are random, there’s no semantic shortcut. The information has to come from the context.

With a typical needle-in-a-haystack test, the needle can stand out from the surrounding text. A model might be very good at retaining that unusual sentence without being equally good at accessing arbitrary information. Here, every entry looks equally relevant, and you don’t know which one will be queried until the end.

I wouldn’t say it measures everything you want from long context. Retrieval isn’t the same as reasoning across a whole codebase. But it’s a clean test of a basic prerequisite: is that context actually accessible to the model, or can it merely accept that many tokens?

r001.rationale: It says the random associations offer “no semantic shortcut,” so the answer must come from information in the context.

r002.rationale: It discusses accessing information throughout the context, but does not identify context coverage and sequential retrieval hops as the central quantitative dimensions.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes retrieval from reasoning across a codebase, but does not say that domain-specific evaluations better measure those abilities.

sol-6.1.text:
The nice thing about hashes is that they’re essentially unpredictable. You can’t infer the answer from your knowledge of the world or from what would be a plausible continuation. You actually have to find the relevant information in the context and return it accurately.

That makes it a clean way to test whether the model can access information across a long context, rather than just accept a lot of tokens as input. And you can vary where the information appears and how much context surrounds it, with an answer that’s straightforward to verify.

I’d qualify “general-purpose,” though. It’s a useful test of whether the context is accessible; it doesn’t, by itself, establish that the model can reason well over everything in that context.

r001.rationale: It says hashes are unpredictable, so the answer cannot be inferred from world knowledge or plausible continuation; the relevant information must be found in the context.

r002.rationale: It mentions varying where information appears and how much context surrounds it, but does not identify sequential retrieval hops as a central dimension.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes context access from broad reasoning ability, but does not contrast general-purpose evaluation with domain-specific evaluations.
